query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under elevated-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) to oxidizing or reducing gases, the degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by whether a stable Al–Cr-enriched oxide scale can form and remain protective. In oxidizing atmospheres above a threshold partial pressure of oxygen, Al and Cr synergistically promote a continuous spinel-like oxide film that impedes further corrosion and preserves the fcc matrix, whereas in reducing or low-oxygen environments, incomplete or nonprotective scaling leads to rapid sub-surface attack, microstructural destabilization, and loss of mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: As-printed (or homogenized) Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a primarily single-phase fcc matrix and minimal precipitation from additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to controlled gas environments (varying O2/H2 partial pressures) at 700–900 °C, with in situ tracking via XRD, EBSD, and thermogravimetric analysis supported by CALPHAD-based thermodynamic simulations.
generation.conditions: Systematically modulate oxygen activity (1–10−6 bar) and temperature (700–900 °C) to emulate both oxidizing and reducing service conditions over 100+ hours, ensuring baseline mechanical properties remain within acceptable limits for structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Preferential formation (or lack) of a continuous Al–Cr-rich oxide scale on the alloy surface, which can inhibit or permit deeper microstructural damage.
generation.mechanism: When the local oxygen partial pressure is sufficient, Al and Cr partition to the surface to form a coherent oxide scale. This prevents further diffusion of oxygen and preserves the fcc matrix. Under reducing or subcritical O2 conditions, significant scale breakdown and localized infiltration of reactive species cause sub-surface phase transformations and cracking, accelerating alloy degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: In strongly oxidizing conditions, surface oxides remain protective, oxidation kinetics remain low, and post-exposure mechanical performance is near-baseline. Under reducing conditions or at very low O2 partial pressures, more rapid mass gain, sub-surface reactions, and mechanical property loss are observable.
generation.baseline: Unexposed or mildly exposed specimens exhibiting stable fcc microstructure and known tensile/fatigue properties in neutral/inert environments at 700–900 °C.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is most relevant to service temperatures of 700–900 °C under controlled partial pressures of oxygen/hydrogen. At substantially higher temperatures or extreme environment changes, other degradation mechanisms (e.g., liquation or nitridation) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold oxygen activity required to stabilize the protective Al–Cr oxide scale remains unknown, and the roles of Ti partitioning and potential minor phases in the scale are not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Run parallel exposures of identically prepared samples at identical temperatures, but with O2 partial pressures spanning a wide range from strongly reducing to strongly oxidizing. Continuously monitor scale formation by in situ diffraction and mass change. After exposure, perform cross-sectional microscopy to assess oxide scale continuity and sub-surface damage.
measurements: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction patterns and electron backscatter diffraction
Cross-sectional SEM/EDS maps of oxide layers and underlying microstructures
Hardness and tensile properties of exposed samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If protective Al–Cr-rich oxides do not form under the predicted oxidizing conditions (above the proposed oxygen partial pressure threshold), or if sub-surface degradation occurs at oxygen partial pressures predicted to be protective, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,].
